newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bulk of Palestinian cabinet submits resignation.
newsitem.headline: Bulk of Palestinian cabinet submits resignation.

text.p: Sixteen of Yasser Arafat's 18 ministers have offered to resign under pressure from Palestinian legislators over alleged corruption and mismanagement of funds.
Agriculture Minister Abdel Jawad Saleh said he and all but two colleagues told Arafat they were ready to quit at a cabinet meeting in the West Bank town of Ramallah on Friday.
"Sixteen ministers submitted their resignation," he said.

It was not clear whether Arafat, already grappling with a grave crisis in the peace process with Israel after a bloody suicide bombing by Islamist militants in Jerusalem, would accept the resignations.

"Some ministers submitted their resignations and asked President Arafat to consider these resignations at a suitable time," Arafat's office said in a statement. His office declined to give further details.
Another minister, who asked not to be identified, denied that the resignations came in response to internal and international pressure on Arafat to root out graft and incompetence.

"We placed our resignations at the disposal of President Arafat in order to find a way to make reforms," the minister said. "It is just a way to deal with problems since we take the issues seriously."
The Palestinian Legislative Council gave Arafat one month on Thursday to dissolve his cabinet, voting 56-1 to appoint a new administration made up of "qualified and experienced ministers".
Their overwhelming vote, which is non-binding, followed a damning report from a panel of nine legislators detailing instances of alleged corruption in Palestinian self-rule areas.

It recommended putting on trial two ministers, one of whom, Planning Minister Nabil Shaath, was not at Friday's cabinet. Shaath, a senior PLO negotiator with Israel, has branded the allegations slander and threatened to sue.
Saleh said Shaath and Information Minister Yasser Abed Rabbo were the two cabinet members who did not offer to resign.

Evidence of apparent corruption and mismanagement by ministers and officials in the Palestinian Authority has deepened resentment and frustration among ordinary Palestinians grappling with economic hardships.

It has also proven an embarrassment for Arafat with international donors, including the European Union and the United States, who have disbursed $1.5 billion in aid since the PLO's interim peace deals with Israel in 1993.
U.S. aid has accounted for $260 million of the total.

Further U.S. disbursements under a five-year, $500 million plan starting in 1994 will depend on whether Congress extends a bill facilitating dealings with the PLO after it returns from its summer break on September 2.
A senior official from the donor community said the International Monetary Fund had been urging Arafat to reshuffle his cabinet so that foreign aid could continue to flow in.
But the official said the resignations would primarily help Arafat with his own people.
"Domestic discontent grew into resentment and Arafat needs a domestic base, so it was natural for him to have some kind of changes," the official said. "He needed to shake the tree."
An official auditor's report earlier this year found the Palestinian Authority had squandered $326 million in 1996. It did not investigate Arafat's office.

The report's findings were the subject of an investigation by a committee appointed by Arafat which reported last week that while money had not been squandered, serious financial, legal and administrative violations had taken place.

The legislators' panel this week specifically recommended putting Shaath and Civilian Affairs Minister Jamil al-Tarifi on trial on suspicion of corruption and misuse of funds. Tarifi has also threatened to sue but was among ministers who offered to step down.
